chunks: Types of motors and their uses. The question: Name a few types of motors. What are they each used for?
There are several kinds of motors, and each is built and driven differently.
The right choice depends on what you need most: simple and cheap, efficient and long-lived, exact position, or running straight from wall-outlet (mains) power.
Knowing the main types lets you pick the right one for a job.
Think of a toolbox. A hammer, a screwdriver and a wrench all turn effort into work, but each is best for a different task. Motors are the same.
A brushed motor is the cheap all-purpose tool, a stepper is the precise one, and a brushless motor is the efficient long-lasting one.
The analogy has one limit: some jobs, like a servo, combine a motor with sensing and control, which is more like a tool with a built-in gauge.
Family tree by supply and commutation. A servo is a layer on top of any of these; it is defined by the feedback loop, not the machine.
Brushed DC motor: spins when you apply DC (steady one-way current, like from a battery), with sliding contacts called brushes switching the coil current.
Brushless DC (BLDC) motor: magnets on the spinning part (rotor), with an electronic controller switching the coils.
Stepper motor: moves in fixed steps, so you can position it without feedback. Servo: a motor plus a sensor and a control loop, so you can command position or speed.
Open loop / closed loop: control without or with feedback from a sensor.
Three jobs, three motors. A toy car wheel only needs to spin, so a cheap brushed motor works. A 3D printer axis must stop at exact spots.
A stepper with 200 steps per turn moves 360° / 200 = 1. 8° per step, with no sensor needed. A drone propeller needs efficiency and long life, so it uses a brushless motor.
That is the whole idea: match the motor type to the need.
"Brushed DC: simple, cheap, voltage sets speed, good for toys, pumps and automotive actuators.
Brushless DC: electronic commutation, efficient and long-lived, used in drones, fans, drives and EVs.
Steppers move in discrete steps with holding torque, so they're used for open-loop positioning such as 3D printers.
AC induction motors run off mains and are rugged, used in appliances and industry. Servos are any motor plus feedback and a control loop for position.
Plus special ones like voice coils and vibration motors. I'd choose based on precision, efficiency, life and cost."
